```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"

```

```{r setup}
library(kmeans625)
```

`kmeans625()` groups the rows of a numeric matrix into `k` clusters
using the standard k-means algorithm (Lloyd's algorithm). It repeats two
steps until the cluster assignments stop changing or until a
pre-specified maximum number of iterations (`iter.max`) is reached:

1.  assign each point to its nearest center;
2.  move each center to the mean of the points assigned to it.

The starting centers are either given by the user or chosen at random
from the rows of the data. Since final cluster assignments vary based on
the starting centers, the algorithm may be repeated `nstart` times and
the partition with the lowest total within-cluster sum of squares
(`tot.withinss`) is selected.

This vignette shows how to use the function, then compares it with
`stats::kmeans()` for correctness and speed.

## Basic usage

To cluster the four measurements in `iris` into three groups:

```{r usage}
x <- as.matrix(iris[, 1:4])
set.seed(625)
fit <- kmeans625(x, centers = 3, iter.max = 50, nstart = 10)
fit$size
fit$centers
```

`centers = 3` asks for three clusters from random starting rows,
`iter.max = 50` allows up to 50 iterations, and `nstart = 10` tries ten
random starts.

The clusters line up closely with the three species:

```{r species}
table(cluster = fit$cluster, species = iris$Species)
```

```{r plot, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 4}
petal <- c("Petal.Length", "Petal.Width")
plot(x[, petal], col = fit$cluster, pch = 16)
points(fit$centers[, petal], pch = 4, cex = 2, lwd = 3)  # centers as crosses
```

`centers` can also be a matrix of starting centers, one row per cluster.
The result is then fully determined, with no randomness:

```{r matrix-centers}
init <- x[c(1, 51, 101), ]
fit2 <- kmeans625(x, centers = init)
fit2$size
```

## Correctness

`stats::kmeans()` uses a different algorithm by default, so the
comparison uses `algorithm = "Lloyd"`. Both functions are given the same
starting centers, so they should return the same result.

With `nstart` of 2 or more, the two functions draw their random starts
differently, so the same seed gives different starting centers; that
case is not compared here.

On `iris`:

```{r correct-iris}
ours <- kmeans625(x, centers = init, iter.max = 50)
ref <- stats::kmeans(x, centers = init, iter.max = 50, algorithm = "Lloyd")

all.equal(ours$cluster, ref$cluster, check.attributes = FALSE)
all.equal(ours$centers, ref$centers, check.attributes = FALSE)
all.equal(ours$withinss, ref$withinss)
all.equal(ours$tot.withinss, ref$tot.withinss)
all.equal(ours$size, ref$size)
all.equal(ours$iter, ref$iter)
```

On simulated data of different sizes, the function below draws `n`
points in `p` dimensions from `k` separated groups, and uses the first
point of each group as its starting center.

```{r sim-data}
sim_data <- function(n, p, k) {
  group <- sample(k, n, replace = TRUE)
  x <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), ncol = p) + 4 * group
  init <- x[match(1:k, group), , drop = FALSE]
  return(list(x = x, init = init))
}
```

```{r correct-sim}
set.seed(625)
settings <- data.frame(n = c(100, 500, 2000), p = c(2, 5, 10), k = c(2, 3, 5))
settings$equal <- NA

for (i in 1:nrow(settings)) {
  d <- sim_data(settings$n[i], settings$p[i], settings$k[i])
  ours <- kmeans625(d$x, centers = d$init, iter.max = 100)
  ref <- stats::kmeans(d$x, centers = d$init, iter.max = 100,
                       algorithm = "Lloyd")
  settings$equal[i] <-
    isTRUE(all.equal(ours$cluster, ref$cluster, check.attributes = FALSE)) &&
    isTRUE(all.equal(ours$centers, ref$centers, check.attributes = FALSE)) &&
    isTRUE(all.equal(ours$tot.withinss, ref$tot.withinss))
}
settings
```

## Efficiency

`bench::mark()` times both functions on simulated data of four sizes,
from 500 to 100,000 rows, from the same starting centers.

```{r bench}
set.seed(625)
sizes <- c(500L, 2000L, 20000L, 100000L)
timings <- data.frame(n = sizes, kmeans625_ms = NA, stats_ms = NA)

for (i in 1:nrow(timings)) {
  d <- sim_data(timings$n[i], p = 5, k = 3)
  res <- bench::mark(
    kmeans625 = kmeans625(d$x, centers = d$init, iter.max = 100),
    stats = stats::kmeans(d$x, centers = d$init, iter.max = 100,
                          algorithm = "Lloyd"),
    check = FALSE,
    filter_gc = FALSE
  )
  # Median time in milliseconds
  timings$kmeans625_ms[i] <- round(as.numeric(res$median[1]) * 1000, 2)
  timings$stats_ms[i] <- round(as.numeric(res$median[2]) * 1000, 2)
}
# How many times slower kmeans625() is
timings$ratio <- round(timings$kmeans625_ms / timings$stats_ms, 1)
timings
```

`stats::kmeans()` is faster, which is expected since it is written and
compiled in C, while `kmeans625()` is written in R. The gap stays at a
few times and does not significantly grow with `n`.
